costliest.narrative: Major flash flooding and debris flows occurred throughout Glenwood Canyon from the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar as a result of significant rainfall from showers and thunderstorms. Multiple mudslides were reported by the Colorado Department of Transportation (CDOT). Numerous vehicles were trapped between slides for several hours. Rainfall rates in excess of 4 inches/hour were estimated with storms. Remote gauges recorded between 1 and 2 inches in less than an hour along the south and east sides of the burn scar. CDOT reported damage to the structure of Interstate 70 which remained closed for over two weeks due to cleanup operations and surveys.

Multiple debris flows occurred along Interstate 70 within the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar between mile marker 123 and Hanging Lake Tunnel. Colorado Department of Transportation (CDOT) described the damage from the new flows as extreme. The new debris piles were around 17 feet tall over the roadway and house-sized boulders fell as well. Hanging Lake trail received considerable damage. At least seven bridges were either destroyed, washed downstream or otherwise severely damaged. National Forest officials say it will be at least late-season 2022 before the trail can be reopened.

Heavy rain formed over the Grizzly Creek burn scar near Glenwood Springs, CO which caused a major mudslide across the Colorado River near MM 124 of Interstate 70. According to CDOT, the material in the river resulted in some damming of the river. Additionally, a smaller mudslide occurred at MM 129 at the same time and flowed across I-70 with an unknown depth. I-70 was closed for an extended period due to cleanup operations.

At least three debris flows of mud, trees and rocks occurred across the eastern portion of the Grizzly Creek Fire burn area near Bair Ranch. Radar estimated 0.30 to 0.50 inches of rain fell in 20 minutes over the affected area. I-70 was closed in both directions for 24 hours due to cleanup operations.

Several debris flows occurred as a result of heavy rain over the western portion of the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar. One debris flow covered both lanes on Interstate 70 and was approximately 80 feet wide and about 5 feet deep. It also ran all the way down to the Colorado River. Radar estimated 0.40 to 0.60 inches of rain fell in 36 minutes. I-70 was closed in both directions for 12 to 24 hours due to cleanup operations.

A debris flow occurred as a result of heavy rain over the western portion of the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar. The debris flow was about 60 to 70 feet wide over the westbound lanes of Interstate 70 and approximately 5 feet deep. A slide at the bottom of the drainage ranged from 6.5 to nearly 8 feet deep. Radar estimated 0.30 to 0.40 inches of rain fell in 20 to 30 minutes. I-70 westbound was closed for several hours due to cleanup operations.

recent.narrative: The San Juan River reached a second crest to major flood stage that was even higher than the first in response to additional significant rainfall and locally heavier rates on October 13. This heavy rainfall was due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Raymond on top of already saturated ground from the previous surge from Tropical Storm Priscilla. The San Juan River climbed back to action stage on October 13 at 1300 MST at 9.48 feet. The second crest reached major flood stage on October 14 at 300 MST at 12.88 feet. The San Juan River then fell below action stage on October 15 at 700 MST.

Significant rainfall fell across the San Juan River Basin between the evening of October 9 and October 11 due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Priscilla. This resulted in major flooding along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs. Action stage of 9.48 feet was exceeded on October 11 at 1100 MST. The San Juan River crested at major flood stage on October 11 at 1600 MST at 12.66 feet and 8270 cfs. The San Juan River then fell to near action stage on October 12 at 1000 MST. Four places were impacted in Archuleta County which were mostly rural. Most of the damage reported were dirt roads washed out and minor flooding to residents where the river exceeded its banks. There were numerous power outages and a water main broke in Pagosa Springs which was repaired on October 12. Preliminary estimates of $5 million to repair man-made white water rapids for kayaking and recreation along the San Juan
